title: O.J. Simpson will not be part of Bills’ Wall of Fame at new Highmark Stadium
content:
The Buffalo Bills’ new stadium will not include any recognition of O.J. Simpson, the first member of the organization’s Wall of Fame.

Debuting this season, Highmark Stadium is set to feature a plaza near its main entrance that the team is calling The Family Circle. Alongside three bison statues will be plaques honoring iconic Bills players. Simpson, who spent nine seasons in Buffalo and still holds multiple franchise records, will not be among them.

“We have made an organizational decision that he is not a fit to display inside our new stadium and family circle,” said Pete Guelli, chief operating officer for the Bills, in a statement.

The Hall of Fame running back was accused in the 1994 double murder of his former wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ron Goldman, but acquitted in a jury trial that lasted eight months and captured the attention of a nation.

Though Simpson walked free, he was later found civilly liable for Goldman’s death and his ex-wife’s battery in 1997 and ordered to pay $33.5 million to their family members. Simpson ultimately paid out very little of that total, but he was later sentenced to 33 years in prison for his role in a 2007 robbery in which he and several other men stole sports memorabilia at gunpoint. He was released on parole in October 2017 and died in 2024 at the age of 76.

For the two decades preceding the Brown and Goldman murder case, Simpson ranked among the nation’s most famous athletes and pop culture figures.

As a star at USC, Simpson led the Trojans to a national championship in 1967 and took home the Heisman Trophy in 1968. The Bills then selected him with the No. 1 pick in the 1969 draft, and he went on to play nine of his 11 pro seasons in Buffalo.

In 1973, Simpson became the first running back to break 2,000 rushing yards in a season, recording 2,003 yards over 14 games. He won both the NFL MVP and Offensive Player of the Year awards that year, and his 1973 per-game rushing average of 143.1 yards stands as an NFL record.

Simpson still holds the Bills’ single-season records for the highest rushing average (6.0 yards), most rushing touchdowns (16) and most total touchdowns (27). A 273-yard Thanksgiving game performance against the Detroit Lions remains the most rushing yards by a Bills player in a single game.

During his 1969-1977 run with the Bills, Simpson played in six Pro Bowls and led the NFL in rushing four times (1972, 1973, 1975 and 1976). He was the NFL’s Player of the Year in 1972, 1973 and 1975, and he made consecutive All-AFC and All-Pro teams from 1972 to 1976. Simpson was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1985.

Joe Buscaglia contributed to this report.
